claims.sentence: Colds and flu are both infections of the airways, and the NHS describes their symptoms as similar.
claims.evidence: UKHSA: flu is a viral infection of nose, throat and lungs; symptoms overlap. No retrieved NHS text says 'the NHS describes symptoms as similar'.
claims.newSentence: Colds and flu are both viral infections that affect the nose and throat, and their symptoms overlap.

claims.sentence: The main difference is how severe they feel.
claims.evidence: UKHSA says a cold is much less severe; nothing ranks severity as 'the main' difference (speed of onset is also a difference).
claims.newSentence: Flu and colds differ in how severe they are and in how quickly they start.

claims.sentence: Flu tends to be more severe than a cold.
claims.evidence: UKHSA: a cold is much less severe than flu; flu usually hits harder.

claims.sentence: A cold mostly affects the nose and throat, while flu can also bring a fever, aches and exhaustion.
claims.evidence: NHS flu page: sudden high temperature, aching body, exhaustion. UKHSA: cold usually runny nose, sneezing, throat irritation, usually no fever or body aches.

claims.sentence: That difference in reach is the most useful clue.
claims.evidence: Opinion. Retrieved text says symptoms overlap and it can be hard or impossible to tell apart by symptoms alone; a test is the only sure way for flu or COVID-19.
claims.newSentence: Because the symptoms overlap, it can be hard to tell flu and a cold apart from symptoms alone.

claims.sentence: A person with a cold usually feels unwell in the nose and throat but is often able to carry on with some normal activity, whereas flu more often leaves a person feeling run down all over.
claims.evidence: NHS flu page: flu can leave you exhausted and too unwell to carry on as normal; a cold usually leaves you unwell but able to manage usual activities. 'Run down all over' and 'often/more often' not stated.
claims.newSentence: With a cold you usually feel unwell but can manage your usual activities, while flu can leave you exhausted and too unwell to carry on as normal.

claims.sentence: Speed of onset is another difference the NHS pages point to.
claims.evidence: NHS flu page contrasts flu appearing quickly with a cold appearing gradually.

claims.sentence: Flu tends to come on suddenly, often within hours.
claims.evidence: NHS flu page: symptoms come on very quickly, within a few hours.

claims.sentence: A cold usually builds more gradually, over about two to three days.
claims.evidence: Retrieved summaries conflict on the timing (one says 2 to 3 days, another 1 to 2 days); only 'gradually' is consistent.
claims.newSentence: A cold usually builds more gradually.

claims.sentence: People often notice a sore throat or a blocked or runny nose first, and other symptoms follow.
claims.evidence: UKHSA lists the main cold signs (blocked or runny nose, sneezing, sore throat, hoarse voice, cough, tired and unwell) but not which comes first.
claims.newSentence: The main signs of a cold are a blocked or runny nose, sneezing, a sore throat, a hoarse voice, a cough, and feeling tired and unwell.

claims.sentence: Most people start to feel better from a cold within about one to two weeks.
claims.evidence: Common cold NHS-sourced text: gets better by itself in a week or two; about a week and a half in adults, up to two weeks in young children.

claims.sentence: Flu usually improves within about a week.
claims.evidence: NHS trust page: you should begin to feel much better within a week or so.

claims.sentence: Tiredness can linger for longer after flu, even when the other symptoms have settled.
claims.evidence: NHS trust page: you may feel tired for much longer.

claims.sentence: Timings vary between people, and the NHS pages for each illness give the usual picture rather than a fixed rule.
claims.evidence: No retrieved text states this about the NHS pages.

claims.sentence: There is no cure for a cold or for flu.
claims.evidence: Not stated in retrieved text. Cold: gets better by itself; flu: antivirals are sometimes prescribed for higher-risk patients, so a blanket claim risks misleading.
claims.newSentence: A cold is caused by a virus and usually gets better by itself.

claims.sentence: The NHS says the usual approach is to rest and drink fluids while the body clears the infection.
claims.evidence: Cold self-care: rest, drink plenty of fluids. Flu NHS trust page: rest, fluids as the main approach.

claims.sentence: Pharmacy medicines can ease symptoms, and a pharmacist can talk through the options.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text backs this for colds only: a pharmacist can recommend suitable cold medicines and check which are safe for you.
claims.newSentence: For a cold, a pharmacist can recommend suitable medicines and check which ones are safe for you.

claims.sentence: Antibiotics do not help, because both illnesses are caused by viruses rather than bacteria.
claims.evidence: Cold: antibiotics do not help because colds are viral. Flu NHS leaflet: antibiotics do not work against the flu virus.

claims.sentence: A flu vaccine protects against flu, but it does not protect against colds.
claims.evidence: Stated by an NHS-affiliated page in the summary but the exact page was not identifiable; plain undisputed fact.

claims.sentence: The NHS separates emergencies from problems that can wait for a call or an appointment.
claims.evidence: NHS flu page separates call 999/A&E from urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

claims.sentence: Sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood is an emergency, and the route is 999 or A&E.
claims.evidence: NHS flu page: call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, or coughing up blood.

claims.sentence: For less urgent worries, NHS 111 or the GP can advise.
claims.evidence: NHS flu page: urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 for listed situations.

claims.sentence: The NHS gives these as reasons to get in touch: symptoms that get worse, a high temperature that lasts for more than three days, symptoms that carry on beyond about ten days, or a cough that continues for more than three weeks.
claims.evidence: Cut-offs (3 days, 10 days, 3 weeks) come from the cold advice only; the flu page gives different wording (not improved after 7 days, very unwell, short of breath). Presenting them as a single NHS list is a cut-off statement that could mislead.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if you have flu symptoms and feel very unwell, are short of breath, or are not getting better.

claims.sentence: People with long-term conditions such as diabetes, asthma or heart disease are advised to seek advice sooner, because flu and colds can hit them harder.
claims.evidence: NHS flu page lists people aged 65 or over, pregnant people, and those with a long-term condition or weakened immune system for urgent GP or NHS 111 advice. Named conditions and 'colds' not backed for this advice.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says people aged 65 or over, people who are pregnant, and people with a long-term condition or a weakened immune system should get an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if they have flu symptoms.

claims.sentence: Other infections can look like flu or a cold.
claims.evidence: UKHSA: COVID-19, RSV, adenovirus and hMPV can cause similar cold-like symptoms.

claims.sentence: The UKHSA publishes a guide to the signs and symptoms of flu, COVID-19 and colds, and the NHS pages for each illness set out what to look for.
claims.evidence: UKHSA blog 'Do I have flu, COVID-19 or a cold? Know the signs and symptoms'; NHS flu and common cold pages exist and list symptoms.

claims.sentence: When symptoms are unusual, severe or not settling as expected, the safest step is to ask NHS 111 or the GP rather than to guess from a list of symptoms.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text says only a test confirms flu or COVID-19, and NHS advises 111/GP when very unwell, short of breath or not improving; 'unusual' and 'safest step' are not stated.
claims.newSentence: Symptoms overlap, so the only way to know for sure whether you have flu or COVID-19 is a test.

claims.sentence: Cold and flu symptoms overlap, but flu tends to be more severe and often comes on within hours.
claims.evidence: UKHSA symptoms overlap and cold much less severe; NHS flu page: within a few hours.

claims.sentence: A cold mainly affects the nose and throat and builds up over a couple of days.
claims.evidence: 'Couple of days' conflicts across retrieved summaries; only 'gradually' is consistent.
claims.newSentence: A cold mainly affects the nose and throat and builds up gradually.

claims.sentence: Neither illness has a cure, and antibiotics do not work against either.
claims.evidence: 'No cure' not stated; antibiotics part is supported (cold page; flu leaflet).
claims.newSentence: Antibiotics do not work against colds or flu, because both are caused by viruses.

claims.sentence: Sudden chest pain, severe breathlessness or coughing up blood needs 999 or A&E.
claims.evidence: NHS flu page: call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe breathing difficulty, or coughing up blood.

claims.sentence: NHS 111 or a GP can advise if symptoms get worse or last longer than expected.
claims.evidence: Cold: seek advice if symptoms get worse or do not improve; flu: GP or 111 if worse or not improved.

claims.sentence: Flu tends to start faster and feel worse than a cold, with fever, aches and exhaustion; a cold mostly stays in the nose and throat.
claims.evidence: NHS flu page: comes on quickly, high temperature, aching body, exhaustion; UKHSA: cold milder, nose and throat.

notes: Searches returned blended summaries; the NHS flu and cold pages were attributed only where the summary tied the point to that page. The cold 'onset' timing was inconsistent across summaries (1 to 2 days vs 2 to 3 days), so numbers were dropped. The 3 day / 10 day / 3 week cut-offs belong to cold advice and should not be presented alongside flu. c19 textbook because the source page could not be identified. Draft's first-pass ledger cited only the two NHS URLs for every sentence.
